name: Patricia Treib
bio: Patricia Treib was born in 1979 in Saginaw, Michigan, and lives and works in Brooklyn. She received a BFA from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago (2001) and an MFA from Columbia University (2006), where she held the Agnes Martin Fellowship. She attended Skowhegan in 2011, held the Marie Walsh Sharpe Space Program studio (2007–08), was a fellow at the American Academy in Rome (2017), and received an Artadia Award (2017). Her paintings take a personal source, such as the outline of a sleeve in a Piero della Francesca fresco, a torsion pendulum clock, a 1940s Vogue sewing pattern or the contours of a 35 mm camera, and rework it into large, open abstractions of flat, interlocking shapes in thinned colour. She has shown with Tibor de Nagy and Wallspace in New York, Golden Gallery in Chicago, Galerie Nordenhake in Stockholm and Mexico City, and Kate MacGarry in London, where Enfold (2024) was her third solo exhibition.
studyNotes: Start from a source you have a personal connection to, then make it unreadable. A sleeve, a cornice, a ribbon or a camera gives the shapes their contours, but the finished picture should not let you name the object. Her real subject, in Kate MacGarry's words, is 'the process of looking'.

Rehearse on paper, then paint the canvas in one go. Each large canvas grows out of several hand-held works on paper made through 'varied repetition', sometimes over years and out of sequence. Once the composition is ready she paints the canvas in a single day, so the result is 'an accumulation of rehearsals' that still looks spontaneous.

Paint flat on the floor with wide brushes and thin paint. She lays the canvas down and uses wide hake brushes and thinned-down washes, erasing and repeating a gesture until each mark fits the next. Try one-stroke shapes made with a brush as wide as the shape itself.

Treat the gaps as forms. The spaces between shapes become primary motifs, and peripheral details move to the centre. Compare Batignolles (2015) with Embrace II (2019) and look at how much of each picture is negative space holding the positive shapes together.

Leave the ground showing. Washes sit on a light, visible ground, so colour stays luminous and every edge reads as a single decision. The 'initial impression of spontaneity' rests on a 'measured and deliberate internal structure'.
